alternates.speaker: Bharat
alternates.setting: After fourteen years, Hanuman brings Bharat the news that Ram is coming; Bharat has one question.
alternates.sanskrit: तब हनुमंत नाइ पद माथा। कहे सकल रघुपति गुन गाथा॥ कहु कपि कबहुँ कृपाल गोसाईं। सुमिरहिं मोहि दास की नाईं ॥
alternates.line: Tell me: does he ever think of me?
alternates.translation: Then Hanuman bowed at his feet and told all of Raghupati's virtues. 'Tell me, Hanuman: does the kind master ever remember me, as one remembers a servant?'

alternates.speaker: Arjuna
alternates.setting: Arjuna asks what becomes of someone who tries and fails; Krishna reassures him.
alternates.sanskrit: अर्जुन उवाचअयतिः श्रद्धयोपेतो योगाच्चलितमानसः । अप्राप्य योगसंसिद्धिं कां गतिं कृष्ण गच्छति ॥
alternates.line: What happens to someone who believes, tries, slips, and doesn't make it to the end?
alternates.translation: Arjuna said: One who has faith but does not strive enough, whose mind falls away from yoga before reaching perfection, what end does he come to, Krishna?
alternates.why: No sincere effort is wasted; you pick up where you left off.

prasang.title: What becomes of one who falls from yoga
prasang.summary: Arjuna fears that one who falls short is lost like a torn cloud. Krishna promises that no one who does good comes to ruin; past effort carries forward and they strive again.
prasang.lesson: No sincere effort is wasted; you pick up where you left off.

verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: After the story of two grieving brothers, Vasishtha tells Rama how worry feeds itself.
verse.sanskrit: चिन्तनेनैधते चिन्ता त्विन्धनेनेव पावकः । नश्यत्यचिन्ततेनैव विनेन्धनमिवानलः ॥
verse.line: Worry grows when you feed it thought, like fire with fuel. Starve it, and it dies down.
verse.translation: Worry grows by thinking, as fire grows with fuel; and it dies by not being thought, as fire dies without fuel.
verse.why: Grief is love; endless rumination is the part we can learn to stop feeding.

prasang.title: Punya consoles his younger brother Pavana after their parents die
prasang.summary: Two brothers live with their parents by the Ganga. When their father and mother die, the elder, Punya, performs the rites calmly while the younger, Pavana, wanders the forest weeping. Punya gently helps him see that the bonds of 'mine' and 'not mine' are made in the mind. Vasishtha draws the lesson: worry grows when fed, and a full mind finds the world full.
prasang.story_hook: When their parents died, one brother quietly lit the funeral fires and the other ran weeping into the forest.
prasang.lesson: Grief is love; endless rumination is the part we can learn to stop feeding.

why: Worry grows when you feed it (Yoga Vasishtha 5.21.6)
worry is shown to live on the attention it is fed

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse.sanskrit: यतो यतो निश्चरति मनश्चञ्चलमस्थिरम् । ततस्ततो नियम्यैतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत् ॥
verse.line: Wherever the restless mind wanders, gently bring it back. Again and again.
verse.translation: Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders, from there one should draw it back and bring it under the control of the self.
verse.why: Moderation and gentle return, again and again, settle the mind.

prasang.title: Meditation in detail
prasang.summary: Krishna describes meditation: moderation in food and sleep, the mind like a lamp in a windless place, bringing the wandering mind back, and feeling others' joy and pain as one's own.
prasang.lesson: Moderation and gentle return, again and again, settle the mind.

verse.meaning: Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders, one should restrain it and bring it back under the self's control. The mind turns outward to sounds and objects. Seeing that cause as unreal, one restrains the mind and settles it under the sway of the self.
verse.for_you: The mind wanders and you feel it. That is the work. You see the pull and you bring it back. Again and again.

why: each time the mind runs to a worry it can be brought back

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From the section on wealth: on keeping your dignity before the rich.
verse.sanskrit: यद्धात्रा निजभालपट्टलिखितं स्तोकं महद्वा धनं तत् प्राप्नोति मरुस्थलेऽपि नितरां मेरौ ततो नाधिकम् । तद्धीरो भव वित्तवत्सु कृपणां वृत्तिं वृथा मा कृथाः कूपे पश्य पयोनिधावपि घटो गृह्णाति तुल्यं जलम् ॥
verse.line: A pot draws the same water from a well or the ocean. Keep your dignity before the rich.
verse.translation: Whatever wealth, small or great, the Creator has written on your forehead, you will get it even in a desert, and no more even on Mount Meru. So be steady; do not play the beggar before the rich for nothing. Look: a pot draws the same water from a well as from the ocean.
verse.why: Money changes how others see you, not who you are. Give it, enjoy it, or lose it.
verse.misuse: Not a reason to stop working or asking for fair pay; a reason not to grovel.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On wealth
prasang.summary: A wry look at money: how the world flatters the rich and forgets the broke, wealth's three destinies, and how distance and neglect ruin what we value. It closes with advice to the chataka bird not to plead before every cloud.
prasang.lesson: Money changes how others see you, not who you are. Give it, enjoy it, or lose it.

why: No need to demean oneself before the rich

verse.speaker: Seer
verse.setting: How a householder becomes a 'world' for others.
verse.sanskrit: यन्मनुष्यान्वासयते यदेभ्योऽशनं ददाति तेन मनुष्याणामथ यत्पशुभ्यस्तृणोदकं विन्दति तेन पशूनां यदस्य गृहेषु श्वापदा वयाꣳस्या पिपीलिकाभ्य उपजीवन्ति तेन तेषां लोको
verse.line: Feed people, find water for animals; when even ants live off your home, you become a world for them.
verse.translation: By housing people and giving them food, he becomes a world for people. By finding grass and water for animals, he becomes a world for animals. When beasts, birds and even ants live off his house, he becomes a world for them.

matched.label: I want to feel more grateful

why: a household is seen as something many lives rest on

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.sanskrit: परिभ्रमसि किं मुधा क्वचन चित्त विश्राम्यतां स्वयं भवति यद्यथा भवति तत्तथा नान्यथा । अतीतमननुस्मरन्नपि च भाव्यसंकल्पयन् नतर्कितसमागमाननुभवामि भोगानहम् ॥
verse.line: Why wander, mind? Rest. Not replaying the past, not scripting the future, I take what comes.
verse.translation: Why do you wander about in vain, mind? Rest somewhere. Whatever is to happen happens just as it will, and not otherwise. Not recalling the past, not planning the future, I enjoy the pleasures that come to me unlooked-for.
verse.why: Stop seeking approval and rehearsing outcomes; the calm you want is already inside.
verse.misuse: Not an argument against planning; it is for the worry loop once you have done your part.

prasang.title: Vairagyashatakam: Advice to the mind
prasang.summary: The poet talks to his own mind: why exhaust yourself pleasing others, why replay the past and script the future, why roam everywhere but within. 'So what?' asks what all our gains amount to.
prasang.lesson: Stop seeking approval and rehearsing outcomes; the calm you want is already inside.

story.title: Kashyapa and the jackal: the gift of hands
story.story_hook: Lying in the dust where a rich man's chariot had thrown him, Kashyapa wanted to die, and a jackal laughed at him.
story.summary: A young brahmin, Kashyapa, knocked down by a rich man's chariot, wants to die in humiliation. A jackal tells him how lucky he is to have hands and a human life, and that craving grows like fire fed with wood. The jackal is Indra.
story.lesson: You already have what others long for. Craving is a fire that more fuel only feeds.
